hints: Look for a carbon with four single bonds to four completely different groups, remembering that carbons in C=C bonds or C=O bonds cannot be chiral.
walkthrough:
Apply the test for chirality**
Picture yourself sitting with the structure. A chiral centre is simply a carbon with four single bonds to four different atoms or groups. So quickly rule out every $\text{C}$ in a $\text{C=C}$ bond, every $\text{C}$ in $\text{C=O}$, and any $\text{C(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ carbon with two identical methyl groups.

Find the only carbon that passes**
Check the ring junction carbon that carries the $-\text{OH}$ group and the unsaturated side-chain. It is bonded to: $-\text{OH}$, the side-chain, one ring $\text{CH}_{2}$ side and one ring $\text{C(CH}_{3}\text{)}$ side. Those are four different groups, so this is the only chiral centre. No other carbon qualifies.
Final answer: Label the tertiary alcohol carbon in the ring, the ring $\text{C}$ bonded to $-\text{OH}$ and to the side-chain.

hints: Start from $\text{C}_{15}\text{H}_{20}\text{O}_{4}$ for abscisic acid and count how many $\text{H}$ atoms are added and whether any $\text{O}$ atoms are lost or gained in this reduction.
walkthrough:
Track atoms through the reduction**
Think of reduction here as addition of hydrogen across a $\text{C=O}$ or $\text{C=C}$ bond. The carbon skeleton stays $\text{C}_{15}$ and the oxygen count stays $\text{O}_{4}$ because no $\text{O}$ is lost as water in this step.

Add the hydrogens**
One double bond reduced consumes one $\text{H}_{2}$ molecule, so $\text{H}_{20} + \text{H}_{2}$ gives $\text{H}_{22}$. That gives $\text{C}_{15}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{4}$.

hints: Recall that vigorous oxidation cleaves each C=C bond and converts each substituted alkene carbon into a carbonyl or carboxyl carbon, so focus on the large ring-containing fragment.
walkthrough:
See what vigorous oxidation does**
Keep this picture in mind. Cold dilute $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ would just add $-\text{OH}$ groups, but hot concentrated acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ cuts right through every $\text{C=C}$ bond. Each $=\text{CH}-$ becomes $-\text{COOH}$ or $\text{CO}_{2}$, each $=\text{C(CH}_{3}\text{)}-$ becomes a methyl ketone $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C=O}-$.

Keep the big piece**
The ring plus its gem-dimethyl groups and its ketone survives as one large piece, but where the ring $\text{C=C}$ and the side-chain $\text{C=C}$ were cut you now draw $\text{C=O}$ and $-\text{COOH}$ groups. That ring-derived keto-diol-diacid is the product of largest molecular mass.

Final answer: Draw the largest $M_{r}$ fragment containing the substituted six-membered ring residue with its two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups, the tertiary $-\text{OH}$, the ring $\text{C=O}$, and two $-\text{COOH}$ groups formed by cleavage of the $\text{C=C}$ bonds.

hints: Identify which alkene carbon in abscisic acid bears only H atoms apart from the double bond, so cleavage there must give a one-carbon fragment.
Recall what happens to an aldehyde intermediate under hot acidified oxidising conditions.
walkthrough:
Spot the one-carbon fragment**
Look for a $=\text{CH}-$ carbon that will be cut off as $\text{HCHO}$ or $\text{HCOOH}$ on initial cleavage. Under the vigorous hot acid conditions this $\text{C}_{1}$ aldehyde or methanoic acid intermediate does not survive.

Oxidise it all the way**
Remember, aldehydes are very easily oxidised to carboxylic acids, and methanoic acid $\text{HCOOH}$ is oxidised further to $\text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. That complete oxidative cleavage is why the smallest molecular mass product isolated is $\text{CO}_{2}$.
Final answer: Smallest product is $\text{CO}_{2}$.\nIt is formed by oxidation / oxidative cleavage of an aldehyde intermediate formed on cleavage of a $\text{C=C}$ bond.

hints: Focus on the side-chain $\text{C(CH}_{3}\text{)=CH-COOH}$ unit and apply the rule that $=\text{C(CH}_{3}\text{)}-$ gives a $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C=O}-$ end after oxidative cleavage.
walkthrough:
Cut the side-chain alkene**
Take the $\text{-C(CH}_{3}\text{)=CH-COOH}$ part of the side-chain. Cleavage of the $\text{C=C}$ bond splits it into two carbonyl pieces. The left-hand $\text{C(CH}_{3}\text{)}$ end becomes $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-C(=O)-}$ and the right-hand $\text{CH}$ end attached to $-\text{COOH}$ becomes $\text{O=CH-COOH}$ initially.

Join the logic to pyruvic acid**
In this particular cleavage both carbons stay joined in the observed $\text{C}_{3}$ keto-acid, pyruvic acid. Writing it clearly gives $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCO}_{2}\text{H}$, which is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-C(=O)-C(=O)-OH}$.
